newsitem.title: UK: Fraught Northern Ireland parade planned for Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Fraught Northern Ireland parade planned for Saturday.

text.p: A Protestant parade which was rerouted when sectarian violence swept Northern Ireland in August has been rescheduled to take place on Saturday amid new communal tension.

Organisers said the Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order, planned to march round the walls of Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city and a stronghold of Irish Catholic nationalists, on Saturday morning.

The plan was immediately condemned by residents of the Catholic Bogside area of Londonderry whose opposition to the original march led to it being rerouted away from the walls which overlook their homes.
Police said they had received a request for permission to hold the march on the walls and were studying it.
It would take place two weeks after the Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombed Britain's army base in Northern Ireland in the first attack in the province in two uneasy years.

The attack, which killed one British soldier, raised fears that Protestant Loyalists would end their own two-year truce to avenge violence by the IRA, which draws its support from the Catholic, Irish nationalist community.
The Apprentice Boys trace their origin to the 17th century when trainee workers slammed shut the gates of Londonderry to keep out an invading Catholic monarch, King James the second.

They march every year but this year's parade was rerouted when Protestant and Catholic violence erupted over the holding of another Protestant parade by the Orange Order through a Catholic area of the southern town of Portadown.
Protestants brought the province to a standstill with demonstrations and impromptu barricades across major roads, igniting a wave of Catholic anger and similar protests.

British troops and police blocked off the walls of Londonderry with huge slabs of concrete and iron fencing to prevent the march taking place and its organisers paraded elsewhere but vowed to return when the time was right.
A spokesman for the Bogside residents, Donnacha MacNiallais, said he saw the planned parade as a confrontation with local Catholics who see such demonstrations as intimidation.
He said he had hoped the organisers would discuss the planned march with his organisation to try to avoid a showdown.
"I regret that the Apprentice Boys did not take up an offer from us in the aftermath of August to sit down and attempt to resolve this issue once and for all.
"But it is still not too late to do that, despite the fact that that process has been made more difficult by them filing for what is essentially a confrontational parade," he said.
The mayor of Londonderry, Richard Dallas, himself a member of the Apprentice Boys, said it was intended to be a small march and he hoped it would pass off without incident.

"I would hope that the parade, which is at 9.30 AM and which is of limited numbers, can pass off peacefully," said Dallas, who is also a member of the Ulster Unionist Party, the main voice of the pro-British Protestant majority.
"That is the intention of the Apprentice Boys. It is not triumphalism, it is simply our wish to express our culture, a wish we were denied last August 10," he said.
